newsitem.title: USA: NASD okays plan to restructure boards.
newsitem.headline: NASD okays plan to restructure boards.

text.p: The National Association of Securities Dealers said Thursday its board has approved a plan to reduce the number of directors in its two units, a move aimed at streamlining decision making.
The plan calls for an interlocking structure, with both the Nasdaq and NASD Regulation boards shrinking in size and becoming part of an expanded NASD parent board, it said.
Frank Zarb, NASD chairman and chief executive officer, said the proposed changes "will enhance the core corporate governance principles put in place last year by creating a more efficient structure."

Under the plan, the total number of directors will be reduced to 17 from 48. The number of board committes will also be reduced to five, from nine, and board meetings will be less frequent -- seven instead of 17 annually.
The proposed changes are subject to approval by NASD members and the Securities and Exchange Commission, which has oversight powers over the self-regulatory organization.
The NASD said its board will maintain a majority of non-industry members while the two subsidiary boards will be balanced between industry and non-industry representatives.
The NASD board, currently with 10 directors, will increase to 27 members.

Its non-industry or independent majority will include at least four public governors, a representative from the Nasdaq-listed companies, a representative each from the mutual fund and insurance industries.
NASD said its board will retain ultimate policymaking, oversight and corporate authority as the parent holding company.
Brokerage regulator NASD Regulation's board, which currently has 24 members, will have five to eight members, with each serving a three-year term.
The board will remain primary responsible for all brokerage industry regulatory matters, but may it may take decisions directly to the parent board.
The Nasdaq, with 16 members currently, will also shrink to between five and eight members. It will continue to have primary authority for market-related rulemaking.

Rule changes made by the Nasdaq board, such as those on fees or other charges, will be subject to review and ratification by the parent board. Members will serve three-year terms and also be members of the parent board.
A single NASD board executive committee will be created to replace the two subsidiary executive committees and this committee will also have a non-industry majority.
A National Adjudicatory Council will be created to replace the current National Business Conduct Committee. The NAC, which will have 12 members, will review decisions such as disciplinary orders.
